items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The shared exercise of decision-making authority by states within a supranational body such as the EU"?

items.stem: Leila writes: "Sovereignty means a state can do anything it wants internationally." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Sovereign states are bound by treaties they sign and by customary international law (e.g. the ban on genocide), and their actions are constrained by the power of others.
items.markingKey: Sovereign states are bound by treaties they sign and by customary international law (e.g. the ban on genocide), and their actions are constrained by the power of others. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why Westphalian sovereignty has always been partly a myth.
items.answer: Powerful states have regularly intervened in weaker ones (colonialism, Cold War interventions, conditional loans), and states voluntarily limit sovereignty through treaties, so non-interference has never been absolute (Krasner). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Powerful states have regularly intervened in weaker ones (colonialism, Cold War interventions, conditional loans), and states voluntarily limit sovereignty through treaties, so non-interference has never been absolute (Krasner). items.stem: Using Krasner's four types of sovereignty, explain which type is weakened when a state cannot stop illegal migration and drug smuggling across its borders.
items.answer: Interdependence sovereignty – the ability to control flows of people, goods and capital across borders; legal recognition (international legal sovereignty) is unaffected.
items.markingKey: Interdependence sovereignty – the ability to control flows of people, goods and capital across borders; legal recognition (international legal sovereignty) is unaffected.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Every state is equal in law, but not in power. The Charter promises non-interference; the history of the last century is a list of interventions."
— Lecture on international law and sovereignty, 2021 (adapted)

Explain, with reference to the source, the gap between sovereignty in law and in practice.
items.answer: Legally states are equal and protected by non-interference (Art. 2(7), 2(4)), but in practice powerful states intervene (e.g. Iraq 2003, Cold War interventions), so sovereignty is unevenly protected.
items.markingKey: Legally states are equal and protected by non-interference (Art. 2(7), 2(4)), but in practice powerful states intervene (e.g. Iraq 2003, Cold War interventions), so sovereignty is unevenly protected. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"In Taiwan there is a government, an army, a currency and free elections. What is missing is a seat at the United Nations."
— Article on contested statehood, 2023 (adapted)

With reference to the source, distinguish between de facto and de jure sovereignty.
items.answer: Taiwan has de facto sovereignty – effective government, army, currency, elections – but lacks de jure recognition by most states and UN membership (UNGA Resolution 2758, 1971 seated the PRC).
items.markingKey: Taiwan has de facto sovereignty – effective government, army, currency, elections – but lacks de jure recognition by most states and UN membership (UNGA Resolution 2758, 1971 seated the PRC). items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Westphalian sovereignty is still the foundation of the international order."
items.answer: Sovereignty remains the organising principle of law and diplomacy, but it is increasingly qualified in practice, so it is a foundation under pressure rather than a fiction.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: UN Charter based on sovereign equality; states guard non-intervention (China, Russia, African states); borders rarely change by force. Arguments against: globalization and supranational bodies limit control; R2P and humanitarian intervention; non-state actors and cyber operations cross borders. Supported judgement: Sovereignty remains the organising principle of law and diplomacy, but it is increasingly qualified in practice, so it is a foundation under pressure rather than a fiction.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that de facto control matters more than legal recognition for a state's sovereignty?
items.answer: Effective control is necessary to govern, but recognition is required for full participation and security; both are needed for complete sovereignty.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Taiwan and Somaliland function effectively; Taliban governs Afghanistan regardless. Arguments against: recognition gives access to UN, loans, treaties; unrecognised entities are vulnerable (Nagorno-Karabakh 2023). Supported judgement: Effective control is necessary to govern, but recognition is required for full participation and security; both are needed for complete sovereignty. items.stem: Briefly explain why external sovereignty depends on recognition by other states.
items.answer: External sovereignty is a social and legal status: other states must treat an entity as an equal through diplomatic relations and UN membership; without recognition (e.g. Somaliland) an entity cannot fully participate in international society.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a state can have de jure sovereignty but limited de facto sovereignty.
items.answer: A state may be internationally recognised and hold a UN seat yet not control all its territory – e.g. Somalia, where Somaliland and al-Shabaab control areas, or Mali, where armed groups control the north.

items.stem: Explain the difference between external sovereignty and internal sovereignty.
items.answer: Internal sovereignty is supreme authority within the state over its population and institutions; external sovereignty is independence from outside control and recognition by other states.

Requirements attached to loans or aid, such as IMF demands for fiscal reforms, that limit a state's policy choices
The principle that a state's borders should not be changed by force or without its consent

items.answer: Mobile capital and global markets constrain policy: states compete for investment by lowering taxes and regulation, and bond markets can punish deficits, reducing the practical autonomy of governments.

"We did not lose sovereignty in Brussels; we shared it, and in sharing it we gained a seat at the table where the rules of our single market are written."

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "All humanitarian interventions are illegal because they breach sovereignty." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Interventions authorised by the UN Security Council under Chapter VII (e.g. Libya, Resolution 1973) are legal; only unauthorised interventions such as Kosovo 1999 are legally contested.

items.stem: Evaluate the extent to which a supranational organization of your choice limits the sovereignty of its members.
items.answer: E.g. the EU (primacy of law, Commission powers, euro), the WTO (dispute settlement), or ECOWAS (sanctions after coups; Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger announced withdrawal in 2024). Weigh legal constraints against voluntary membership and exit options.

items.stem: Explain why Taiwan has only a small number of formal diplomatic allies.
items.answer: Under the "One China" policy, the PRC requires states to break formal ties with Taiwan before establishing relations, and has used economic incentives to persuade allies to switch (e.g. Honduras in 2023, Nauru in 2024).

items.stem: Explain why recognition of new states is often a political rather than a purely legal decision.
items.answer: Although the Montevideo criteria are legal, each state decides whether to recognise based on its interests and alliances – e.g. most Western states recognise Kosovo, while Russia, China, Spain and others do not, partly fearing precedents for their own secessionist regions.

Supported judgement: Effective control is necessary to govern, but recognition is required for full participation and security; both are needed for complete sovereignty. items.stem: Assess the validity of the claim that humanitarian intervention is a justified exception to state sovereignty.
items.answer: Intervention can be justified in extreme cases when authorised and proportionate, but selectivity and poor outcomes make it a narrow exception.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: sovereignty as responsibility (R2P); Rwanda shows cost of inaction; Kosovo prevented further ethnic cleansing. Arguments against: risk of abuse (Iraq 2003, Libya regime change); selectivity undermines legitimacy; outcomes often worsen (Libya). Supported judgement: Intervention can be justified in extreme cases when authorised and proportionate, but selectivity and poor outcomes make it a narrow exception. items.stem: Which of the following scholars described sovereignty as "organized hypocrisy"?
items.answer: Stephen Krasner
items.markingKey: D. Krasner (1999) identified four meanings: domestic, interdependence, international legal and Westphalian sovereignty.

items.stem: Which of the following countries received three bailouts between 2010 and 2018 from the "troika" of the European Commission, ECB and IMF?
items.answer: Greece
items.markingKey: D. Ireland received one programme; Greece needed three.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "recognition"?
options: The formal acknowledgement by a state that another entity is a state or that a government is its legitimate representative
The formal withdrawal of a territory and its people from an existing state to form a new state
The recognition of a state's independence and equality by other states in the international system
The use of military force by external actors in a state, without its consent, to stop mass atrocities against civilians
items.answer: The formal acknowledgement by a state that another entity is a state or that a government is its legitimate representative
items.markingKey: A. "recognition" is the formal acknowledgement by a state that another entity is a state or that a government is its legitimate representative.

items.stem: Distinguish between de facto sovereignty and de jure sovereignty.
items.answer: De jure sovereignty is legal authority recognised in law; de facto sovereignty is effective control in practice, which may exist without recognition (Taiwan) or be lacking despite recognition (Somalia).
items.markingKey: De jure sovereignty is legal authority recognised in law; de facto sovereignty is effective control in practice, which may exist without recognition (Taiwan) or be lacking despite recognition (Somalia). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between humanitarian intervention and peacekeeping.
items.answer: Humanitarian intervention uses force without the host state's consent to stop atrocities; traditional UN peacekeeping is deployed with the consent of the parties, impartially, using force only in self-defence or defence of the mandate.
items.markingKey: Humanitarian intervention uses force without the host state's consent to stop atrocities; traditional UN peacekeeping is deployed with the consent of the parties, impartially, using force only in self-defence or defence of the mandate. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between external self-determination and internal self-determination.
items.answer: Internal self-determination means a people governing itself within an existing state (autonomy, minority rights, e.g. Scotland's devolved parliament); external self-determination means forming an independent state or choosing a new status (e.g. South Sudan 2011).
items.markingKey: Internal self-determination means a people governing itself within an existing state (autonomy, minority rights, e.g. Scotland's devolved parliament); external self-determination means forming an independent state or choosing a new status (e.g. South Sudan 2011). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why Westphalian sovereignty has always been partly a myth.
items.answer: Powerful states have regularly intervened in weaker ones (colonialism, Cold War interventions, conditional loans), and states voluntarily limit sovereignty through treaties, so non-interference has never been absolute (Krasner).

(2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that self-determination always means the right to secede. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: International law mainly applies external self-determination to colonial peoples or occupied territories; for other groups it is usually interpreted as internal self-determination within existing states.
items.markingKey: International law mainly applies external self-determination to colonial peoples or occupied territories; for other groups it is usually interpreted as internal self-determination within existing states. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Sovereignty means a state can do anything it wants internationally." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Sovereign states are bound by treaties they sign and by customary international law (e.g. the ban on genocide), and their actions are constrained by the power of others.
items.markingKey: Sovereign states are bound by treaties they sign and by customary international law (e.g. the ban on genocide), and their actions are constrained by the power of others. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Poland and Hungary rule-of-law disputes with the EU and explain what it reveals about supranational limits on national sovereignty.
items.answer: The EU launched Article 7 proceedings and in 2022 used the conditionality mechanism to suspend some funds to Hungary over judicial independence and corruption concerns. EU institutions constrained how member states organise their judiciaries, showing pooled sovereignty in practice
items.markingKey: Context (The EU launched Article 7 proceedings and in 2022 used the conditionality mechanism to suspend some funds to Hungary over judicial independence and corruption concerns.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: EU institutions constrained how member states organise their judiciaries, showing pooled sovereignty in practice – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to supranational limits on national sovereignty.

items.stem: Explain why Spain is unlikely to recognise Kosovo, using the concept of precedent.
items.answer: Spain faces secessionist movements in Catalonia and the Basque Country; recognising a unilateral secession could be seen as a precedent legitimising these claims, so it supports Serbia's territorial integrity.
items.markingKey: Spain faces secessionist movements in Catalonia and the Basque Country; recognising a unilateral secession could be seen as a precedent legitimising these claims, so it supports Serbia's territorial integrity.

items.stem: "A state that joins the EU loses all its sovereignty." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: EU members pool sovereignty in specific areas but retain sovereignty over many policies and can leave under Article 50 TEU, as the UK did in 2020.
items.markingKey: EU members pool sovereignty in specific areas but retain sovereignty over many policies and can leave under Article 50 TEU, as the UK did in 2020. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A government says: "We will not let the IMF dictate our budget." Explain how IMF conditionality could challenge its sovereignty, and one way the government might resist.
items.answer: Conditionality requires policy changes (subsidy cuts, tax reform) as a condition of loans, limiting policy autonomy; the government could seek alternative lenders (China, Gulf states), negotiate softer terms or default – as Argentina has repeatedly renegotiated.
items.markingKey: Conditionality requires policy changes (subsidy cuts, tax reform) as a condition of loans, limiting policy autonomy; the government could seek alternative lenders (China, Gulf states), negotiate softer terms or default – as Argentina has repeatedly renegotiated.

items.stem: "Palestine is a full member state of the United Nations." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Palestine has been a non-member observer state since 2012; a US veto in the Security Council blocked full membership in April 2024, although the General Assembly upgraded its rights in May 2024.
items.markingKey: Palestine has been a non-member observer state since 2012; a US veto in the Security Council blocked full membership in April 2024, although the General Assembly upgraded its rights in May 2024. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine as an example, explain violation of external sovereignty and territorial integrity.
items.answer: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and claimed to annex four Ukrainian regions in September 2022; the UN General Assembly condemned the annexations by 143 votes to 5. the invasion breached Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, and most states refused to recognise the annexations
items.markingKey: Context (Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and claimed to annex four Ukrainian regions in September 2022; the UN General Assembly condemned the annexations by 143 votes to 5.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Globalization has weakened state sovereignty more than any other factor."
items.answer: Globalization constrains autonomy, but states retain and reassert authority, and other challenges such as supranational law are more direct legal limits.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: capital mobility and markets constrain policy; global supply chains, digital flows. Arguments against: states shaped globalization through trade agreements; COVID-19 border closures and tariffs show reassertion; supranational bodies and intervention also limit sovereignty. Supported judgement: Globalization constrains autonomy, but states retain and reassert authority, and other challenges such as supranational law are more direct legal limits.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"We meet every criterion of statehood. We have held peaceful elections for three decades. Yet the world prefers the fiction of a united Somalia."
— Statement by a Somaliland official, 2023 (adapted)

With reference to the source, explain why Somaliland's statehood is contested.
items.answer: Somaliland claims to meet the factual criteria (government, elections), but other states and the AU prioritise Somalia's territorial integrity and fear precedents, so it lacks de jure recognition.
items.markingKey: Somaliland claims to meet the factual criteria (government, elections), but other states and the AU prioritise Somalia's territorial integrity and fear precedents, so it lacks de jure recognition. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: "Westphalian sovereignty is still the foundation of the international order." Using one theoretical perspective and relevant case studies, discuss this view.
items.answer: Sovereignty remains the organising principle of law and diplomacy, but it is increasingly qualified in practice, so it is a foundation under pressure rather than a fiction.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: UN Charter based on sovereign equality; states guard non-intervention (China, Russia, African states); borders rarely change by force. Arguments against: globalization and supranational bodies limit control; R2P and humanitarian intervention; non-state actors and cyber operations cross borders. Supported judgement: Sovereignty remains the organising principle of law and diplomacy, but it is increasingly qualified in practice, so it is a foundation under pressure rather than a fiction.
